entities.name: Humboldt University of Berlin
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Humboldt University of Berlin, founded in 1810 by Wilhelm von Humboldt, is the institution that created the modern research university model — combining teaching with original research, graduate seminars, and academic freedom — which became the global standard for higher education. The 'Humboldtian model' diffused worldwide, particularly to American universities, transforming how humanity generates and transmits knowledge.

Wilhelm von Humboldt's founding vision was revolutionary: professors should be active researchers generating new knowledge, not merely transmitting received wisdom; students should participate in research, not just memorize; and the university should be free from state interference in academic inquiry. These principles — Lehr- und Lernfreiheit (freedom to teach and learn) — created the conditions for the extraordinary German scientific dominance of the 19th century.

Humboldt University's faculty reads as a roll call of modern intellectual history: Hegel lectured philosophy; Marx was a student; Einstein taught physics; Max Planck discovered quantum mechanics; Otto von Bismarck studied law. The university was home to 29 Nobel Prize winners including Planck, Einstein, and Hertz. Nazi persecution ended this golden age — nearly a third of faculty were dismissed after 1933, triggering the brain drain to American universities that transferred German scientific leadership to the US. The book burning in Bebelplatz opposite the university (1933) became the symbol of academic freedom under totalitarianism.
